prompt: A node drain is blocked and the maintenance window is closing. Diagnose whether forcing it is safe.
directAnswer: Bind cluster/node UID, cordon state, every resident Pod owner, PDB allowance, local/ephemeral data, topology and volume constraints, replacement scheduling capacity and current user SLI. A blocked eviction is a safety signal, not a nuisance. Classify whether the blocker is zero disruption allowance, unmanaged Pod, local data, unavailable controller, topology/storage constraint or lack of requests-based headroom. Add capacity, restore the owner, reschedule the window or obtain a narrowly reviewed exception. Do not disable all PDBs or force-delete stateful work. Verify replacements become Ready endpoints, user operation remains healthy, node is recovered/un cordoned as planned and temporary exceptions are removed.
foundation: Drain safety depends on eviction eligibility and replacement serving capacity.
reasoningSteps: Choose safe capacity or exception path.
seniorAnswer: I preserve the blocker, because it identifies exactly which availability or data contract the maintenance plan failed to satisfy.
weakAnswer: Use --force and delete emptyDir data because maintenance is approved.
whyWeak: Approval does not establish workload ownership, data disposability or replacement capacity.

followUps.prompt: Does a PDB cover node failure?
followUps.answer: It constrains voluntary disruptions; it cannot prevent involuntary loss.
Scheduling and much autoscaling capacity reasoning uses requests, not observed averages.
